claim_verdicts.evidence: "Operators are software extensions to Kubernetes that make use of custom resources to manage applications and their components. Operators follow Kubernetes principles, notably the control loop." Motivation: "The operator pattern aims to capture the key aim of a human operator who is managing a service or set of services."

"The controller(s) for that resource are responsible for making the current state come closer to that desired state." "Controllers that interact with external state find their desired state from the API server"; "a controller will send messages to the API server that have useful side effects."

Round 2: section 4 now uses the round-1 suggested_text, conditioned on "a controller built this way compares states". controller.md: "The controller(s) for that resource are responsible for making the current state come closer to that desired state." and "Controllers can fail, so Kubernetes is designed to allow for that." A state that still differs is still there to compare; the claim no longer asserts this of every controller.

In other words: access is denied by default." Together: a ServiceAccount may act only where some bound rule grants it. (New claim n=8 in round 2; the old serial-number claim was dropped.)

Captured run: `kubectl auth can-i list secrets -A --as=system:serviceaccount:cert-manager:cert-manager` -> `yes`; same for operator-lessons:default -> `no`. Manifest: controller ClusterRole (component "controller", v1.20.4) has resources ["secrets"] verbs ["get","list","watch","create","update","delete"].

"Every Kubernetes namespace contains at least one ServiceAccount: the default ServiceAccount for that namespace, named `default`. If you do not specify a ServiceAccount when you create a Pod, Kubernetes automatically assigns the ServiceAccount named `default` in that namespace."

Follows from claim 9: the cert-manager controller ClusterRole grants get/list/watch/create/update/delete on secrets, and can-i -A answers yes, so code running as that ServiceAccount can reach Secrets in every namespace regardless of which ones it wrote.
